questions.question: What is the Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) pattern in unit testing?
questions.title: Arrange Act Assert Pattern JUnit | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA)** is a three-phase structure for a test: **Arrange** the inputs and the object under test, **Act** by calling the one method being tested, then **Assert** the observable result. Keeping each phase distinct makes a test read top-to-bottom and ensures it exercises exactly one behavior.

sections.title: The Three Phases of a Test
sections.content: **Arrange-Act-Assert** is the standard skeleton for a readable unit test. **Arrange** sets up everything the test needs — inputs, the object under test, and any stubbed collaborators. **Act** is the single call to the method being tested, capturing its result. **Assert** verifies the observable outcome against the expectation. Separating these phases (often with blank lines or comments) makes the test self-documenting and keeps it focused on **one behavior** — if you find two Act steps, you're probably testing two things and should split the test. AAA is the same idea as BDD's **Given-When-Then**.

sections.title: AAA at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Arrange|~Set the stage|inputs + object under test|stub collaborators|the starting state
blue|Act|~One action|call the method|capture the result|exactly one call
amber|Assert|~Verify outcome|check observable result|against expectation|one behavior
violet|Maps to|~Given-When-Then|Given = Arrange|When = Act|Then = Assert

sections.title: AAA Phase by Phase
sections.content:
| Phase | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Arrange** | What's the starting state? | `var cart = new Cart(); cart.add(book);` |
| **Act** | What action am I testing? | `double total = cart.total();` |
| **Assert** | What should be true after? | `assertThat(total).isEqualTo(10.0);` |

sections.title: A Test Structured with AAA
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Interleaving phases.** Asserting in the middle of setup makes the test hard to follow.
- **Multiple Act steps.** Two actions in one test usually means two behaviors — split them.
- **Arrange bloat.** If setup is huge, extract a helper or fixture; a giant Arrange signals too many dependencies.
- **No clear Assert.** A test that only acts but doesn't assert proves nothing.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Arrange / Act / Assert** — set up, call, verify.
- **One Act** keeps the test focused on a single behavior.
- **Separate phases** with blank lines or comments for readability.
- **Maps to Given-When-Then** in BDD.
- **Big Arrange** is a coupling smell — extract helpers.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Arrange-Act-Assert is the standard way I structure a unit test, and it has three phases. In the Arrange phase I set up everything the test needs — the inputs, the object I'm testing, and any collaborators. In the Act phase I make a single call to the method I'm actually testing and capture its result. And in the Assert phase I check the observable outcome against what I expected.

Keeping those three phases distinct, usually with a blank line or a short comment between them, makes the test read top-to-bottom so anyone can immediately see the setup, the action, and the expectation. For example, in a shopping cart test, I'd arrange by creating a cart and adding two items, act by calling total, and assert that the total is the sum.

The most useful discipline that falls out of this is the single Act. If I notice I have two actions in one test, that's a strong signal I'm testing two different behaviors and I should split it into two tests. That keeps each test failing for exactly one reason, which makes debugging much faster.

AAA is essentially the same idea as Given-When-Then from behavior-driven development — Given is Arrange, When is Act, Then is Assert. Common mistakes are interleaving the phases, having multiple Act steps, and letting the Arrange phase balloon, because a giant setup usually means the class under test has too many dependencies.

questions.question: How do you use assertThrows to test exception scenarios in JUnit 5?
questions.title: assertThrows JUnit 5 Exception Testing | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **`assertThrows(ExpectedType.class, executable)`** runs the executable, passes for the expected type or a subtype, and returns the exception. Keep the executable limited to the operation expected to fail. Inspect a stable message, code, field, or cause only when that detail belongs to the contract; use `assertThrowsExactly` for exact runtime type.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`assertThrows(Type, lambda)`** — accepts the expected type or a subtype and returns the exception.
- **Inspect stable details** — message, code, cause, or field only when it belongs to the contract.
- **Exact type when required** — use `assertThrowsExactly`.
- **Minimal lambda** — keep only the operation expected to fail.
- **`assertDoesNotThrow`** — available when successful completion is itself the behavior being checked.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `assertThrows` runs the supplied lambda and fails when it completes normally or throws an incompatible type. A subtype satisfies `assertThrows`; when exact runtime type is part of the contract, JUnit also has `assertThrowsExactly`. The successful assertion returns the caught exception, so I can inspect a stable error code, message fragment, custom field, or cause when that detail is public behavior. For example, I can assert that `account.withdraw(-10)` throws `IllegalArgumentException` and carries the code `NEGATIVE_AMOUNT`. I keep setup outside the lambda so another call cannot accidentally satisfy the assertion. A hand-written try/catch can be valid, but `assertThrows` is clearer for this common contract and avoids forgetting a `fail()` on the normal path.

sections.title: How assertThrows proves an exception contract
sections.content:
**`assertThrows`** tests an exception as an observable result. JUnit runs only the executable passed to it. The assertion fails when that code completes normally or throws an incompatible type; when it succeeds, it returns the caught exception for further checks.

For example, `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> account.withdraw(-10))` proves the invalid call is rejected. The returned exception can then be checked for a stable message, cause, or domain field. Keep the lambda limited to the one operation expected to fail, because setup code inside the lambda could throw the same type and make a weak test pass. Prefer the most specific exception that forms part of the method contract.

sections.title: assertThrows at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Signature|~Type + lambda|assertThrows(T.class, exec)|fails if not thrown|wrong type also fails
blue|Returns|~The exception|assert getMessage()|assert getCause()|downcast custom fields
amber|Keep small|~Lambda scope|only the throwing call|proves that line threw|not the whole method
violet|Negative case|~assertDoesNotThrow|valid input runs|no exception|completes cleanly

sections.title: Verbose and fragile: try/catch + fail()
Clean and precise: assertThrows
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **try/catch without a failing normal path.** If nothing throws, the test can pass accidentally; `assertThrows` avoids that pattern.
- **Asserting a broad superclass.** Use the most specific exception promised by the contract.
- **Checking unstable details.** Assert a message, code, cause, or field only when it is stable public behavior.
- **Too much in the lambda.** Setup inside the executable can throw the same type and satisfy a weak assertion.

questions.question: What is assertAll in JUnit 5 and when should you use it?
questions.title: assertAll JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`assertAll`** groups executable assertions, normally runs each one, and reports their collected failures together instead of stopping at the first assertion failure. Use it for independent properties of one result. Serious unrecoverable errors can still stop execution, and dependent checks should not assume an earlier assertion passed.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`assertAll`** normally executes each supplied check and aggregates failures.
- **Use for** several independent properties of one object or result.
- **Still one behavior** — not multiple unrelated workflows.
- **No guard assumption** — a later check must not rely on an earlier assertion passing.
- **Add a heading** when it makes the grouped failure easier to locate.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
assertAll lets me group several assertions together so JUnit runs all of them and reports every failure at once, instead of stopping at the first one. Normally, if I have three separate assertEquals calls and the first fails, the test stops right there — I fix it, rerun, and only then discover the second one was also wrong. That's a slow loop. With assertAll, I pass the assertions as a group of lambdas, and a single run tells me everything that's wrong.

Where it shines is verifying several properties of the same object or result. For example, if a method returns a point, I can check x, y, and z inside one assertAll, and if two of them are off, I see both immediately. A useful mental model is multiple aspects of one outcome, not multiple outcomes.

And that distinction is important, because assertAll is not a license to test multiple behaviors in one test. If I'm tempted to check the discount calculation and the inventory update in the same assertAll, those are two behaviors and they belong in two separate tests. The single-responsibility rule for tests still applies — assertAll just helps when one behavior has several observable fields.

One subtle gotcha: the assertions inside assertAll should be independent, because they all run. If a later assertion dereferences something that an earlier not-null check was guarding, you can get a NullPointerException. For those cases I keep the dependent check separate.

sections.title: How grouped assertions are evaluated
sections.content:
A normal failed assertion throws immediately, so the rest of that test method does not run. **`assertAll`** accepts a heading and a group of executable assertions, runs every executable, and reports the collected failures together.

For example, one test may verify the name, email, and status of a newly created `User`. Those checks describe different properties of the same result, so grouping them makes one failure report more useful. It should not combine unrelated effects such as database persistence and email delivery; those are separate behaviors and deserve separate tests. Grouped assertions should also be independent. A later assertion must not assume that an earlier `assertNotNull` succeeded, because JUnit still executes the later assertion.

sections.title: assertAll at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|What it does|~Runs all assertions|reports every failure|no stop at first|grouped
blue|Use for|~One object's fields|x and y of a Point|all DTO properties|complete picture
amber|Not for|~Multiple behaviors|that's separate tests|one behavior per test|don't abuse
violet|Signature|~assertAll(label, ...)|takes Executable lambdas|optional heading|nestable

sections.title: Separate asserts: stop at the first failure
assertAll: report every failure together
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Cramming behaviors in.** `assertAll` is for one result's properties, not for testing discount AND inventory together.
- **Dependent assertions.** If a later check needs an earlier one to hold (e.g. not-null before field access), `assertAll` runs them all and may NPE — keep them independent.
- **Skipping it for objects.** Asserting many fields one-by-one wastes debugging cycles.
- **No label.** A heading makes the grouped failure easier to read.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: `assertAll` gives a fuller failure report for independent properties of one result, but it does not create separate tests and all grouped executables still share the same setup and state. Keep dependent checks outside the group or nest them safely, because one assertion that dereferences null can obscure the useful result.

questions.question: How do you test floating point numbers in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Testing Floating Point JUnit 5 | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: For an approximate floating-point result, use **`assertEquals(expected, actual, delta)`** or AssertJ's **`isCloseTo`** with a tolerance chosen from the domain. Do not copy one epsilon into every test. For exact decimal quantities such as accounting values, use `BigDecimal` or integer minor units when that representation matches the business rules.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Binary floating point is approximate** — many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly.
- **`assertEquals(exp, act, delta)`** — use a tolerance derived from the calculation or domain.
- **AssertJ `isCloseTo(v, within(...))`** — a fluent alternative.
- **Exact decimal requirements** — use `BigDecimal` or integer minor units when the business model requires exact decimal arithmetic.
- **`BigDecimal` comparison** — `equals` includes scale; use `compareTo` when only numerical value matters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The key thing about floating point is that doubles and floats can't represent most decimal numbers exactly, so the arithmetic accumulates tiny rounding errors. The classic example is that zero point one plus zero point two doesn't equal zero point three — it comes out as zero point three followed by a bunch of zeros and a four at the end. So if I write a plain assertEquals expecting zero point three, the test fails, even though the math is conceptually correct.

The fix in JUnit is to use the delta overload of assertEquals, where I pass a third argument that's a small tolerance, like zero point oh oh oh one. That says the values just have to be within that tolerance of each other. AssertJ has the same idea with isCloseTo and within. The thing to be careful about is picking a sensible tolerance — too loose and you start hiding real bugs.

For anything involving money, though, I wouldn't use doubles at all. I'd use BigDecimal, which does exact decimal arithmetic, so there's no drift. The one gotcha there is that BigDecimal's equals method also compares the scale, so zero point three zero is not equal to zero point three by equals. When I'm comparing values, I use compareTo and check it returns zero, which ignores the scale difference.

Common mistakes are comparing doubles without a delta, using an overly large delta, and using doubles for currency.

sections.title: Why decimal-looking values need a tolerance
sections.content:
A `double` stores values in binary, so many ordinary decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly. The calculated result may be extremely close to the expected value without being bit-for-bit equal. JUnit therefore provides `assertEquals(expected, actual, delta)`, where the assertion passes when the difference is within the chosen tolerance.

For example, `assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 1e-9)` allows the tiny representation error but still catches a meaningful calculation error. The delta must come from the precision the application actually needs; an oversized value can hide a bug. Currency is a different case: use `BigDecimal` for exact decimal rules. Remember that `BigDecimal.equals` also compares scale, while `compareTo(...) == 0` compares numerical value.

sections.title: Comparing Decimals at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|The problem|~Doubles aren't exact|0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3|rounding error|plain assertEquals fails
emerald|Fix: delta|~Tolerance overload|assertEquals(exp, act, 0.0001)|small epsilon|JUnit built-in
blue|Fix: AssertJ|~Fluent|isCloseTo(v, within(...))|readable|same idea
violet|Money|~Use BigDecimal|never double for cash|compareTo not equals|exact arithmetic

sections.title: Wrong: exact equality on doubles
Right: delta tolerance, or BigDecimal for money
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Exact comparison for approximate output.** Use a tolerance when the algorithm permits rounding error.
- **Arbitrary epsilon.** Too loose hides bugs; too tight makes tests brittle. Derive it from the requirement.
- **Binary floating point for exact decimal accounting.** Choose a decimal or minor-unit model that matches the money rules.
- **`BigDecimal.equals` when scale is irrelevant.** `equals` distinguishes `0.30` and `0.3`; use `compareTo` when the contract is numerical equality.

questions.question: How do you verify that a list returned by a method has the correct content in JUnit 5?
questions.title: Assert List Contents JUnit 5 | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: To verify a returned list, you can use core JUnit (`assertEquals(expectedList, actual)` for order-sensitive equality, `assertTrue(actual.contains(x))`), but **AssertJ** is far more expressive: `assertThat(list).hasSize(2).containsExactly(a, b)` or `.extracting(Order::id).containsExactlyInAnyOrder(...)`. Choose `containsExactly` (order matters) vs `containsExactlyInAnyOrder` (order doesn't) deliberately.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Don't assert size alone** — verify the actual elements.
- **`containsExactly`** — same elements, same order.
- **`containsExactlyInAnyOrder`** — same elements, order ignored.
- **`extracting(X::field)`** — assert a property across elements.
- **AssertJ** reads better than loops or bare `contains`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Asserting only the size of a list is weak, because a test that just checks the list has two elements still passes if those two elements are completely wrong. So I want to assert the actual contents.

With core JUnit, I can do assertEquals between an expected list and the actual list, which checks equality including order, or I can use assertTrue with contains to check membership. That works, but for collections AssertJ is much more expressive and reads better. I'd write assertThat the list, then chain hasSize and containsExactly with the elements I expect.

The distinction I'm careful about is order. containsExactly means the same elements in the same order, so it fails if the order is different. containsExactlyInAnyOrder means the same elements but order doesn't matter, which is what I'd use for something like a database query result where the order isn't guaranteed. And plain contains just checks that certain elements are present without caring about the rest. Picking the wrong one is a classic source of flaky tests — using containsExactly on an unordered result will fail intermittently.

AssertJ also has extracting, which is really handy. Instead of comparing whole objects, I can extract a property — say the id of each order — and then assert on that list of ids. That's useful when the objects don't override equals, because containsExactly relies on equals. So

sections.title: List content assertions and their contracts
sections.content:
A useful list assertion starts with the method contract: must the order match, must every element match, or does only membership matter? Core JUnit can compare two lists with `assertEquals`, using the lists’ equality rules, which include element order. AssertJ offers more explicit collection checks.

For example, `assertThat(result).containsExactly("A", "B")` proves both contents and order, while `containsExactlyInAnyOrder("A", "B")` proves the same contents when ordering is not part of the contract. `contains("A")` allows extra values and is therefore weaker. For domain objects, `extracting(Order::id)` can compare stable properties instead of relying on whole-object equality. A size-only assertion is not enough: a two-element list can still contain the wrong two elements.

sections.title: Collection Assertions at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Core JUnit|~Basic checks|assertEquals(list, list)|assertTrue(contains)|order-sensitive equals
blue|AssertJ contains|~Order matters|containsExactly(a, b)|exact sequence|fails on wrong order
amber|AssertJ any-order|~Order ignored|containsExactlyInAnyOrder|same set|good for query results
violet|extracting|~Per-property|extracting(Order::id)|across elements|then containsExactly

sections.title: From Weak to Precise Collection Assertions
Which Collection Matcher to Use
sections.content:
| Goal | Matcher | Order sensitive? |
|---|---|---|
| Exact elements, exact order | `containsExactly(a, b)` | Yes |
| Exact elements, any order | `containsExactlyInAnyOrder(a, b)` | No |
| At least these present | `contains(a, b)` | No |
| Just the size | `hasSize(2)` | n/a |
| A field across all | `extracting(X::f).contains(...)` | depends on variant |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only asserting size.** `hasSize(2)` passes with the wrong two elements; assert contents.
- **Wrong order semantics.** Using `containsExactly` on an unordered query result causes flaky failures; use `...InAnyOrder`.
- **Comparing objects without `equals`.** `containsExactly` relies on `equals`; use `extracting` on a key field if not overridden.
- **Manual loops.** Hand-rolled for-loops with asserts are noisy; AssertJ collection matchers are clearer.

- **Exact type** — `assertThrowsExactly` is available when required.
- **Small executable** — setup should not accidentally satisfy the assertion.
- **JUnit 4 comparison** — unlike `@Test(expected=)`, the returned exception can be inspected.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`assertThrows` runs one executable and returns the exception when the expected type or a subtype is thrown. If exact runtime type matters, use `assertThrowsExactly`.

I keep the lambda limited to the operation expected to fail, because setup inside it could throw the same type and make a weak test pass. I then inspect only stable details that belong to the contract. A domain error code may be stronger than an exact message if the message is intended for people and can change. A cause is worth checking when wrapping that cause is part of the behavior.

For example, a withdrawal test can assert `InsufficientFundsException` and then verify its `availableBalance` field. A broad type such as `RuntimeException` usually proves too little, while checking type, full message, cause, and every field without a contract makes the test brittle.

sections.title: Verify the type and the useful exception details
sections.content:
An exception test is strongest when it verifies the full public contract, not merely that some failure happened. **`assertThrows`** accepts an expected class and an executable, then returns the caught exception. Matching includes subclasses, so the expected class should be as specific as the contract allows.

For example, a payment service may throw `PaymentRejectedException` with a stable error code while wrapping a gateway exception as its cause. The test can capture that object, check its code, and check `getCause()` without depending on a full message that contains changing values. Put only `service.pay(request)` inside the lambda so an exception from test setup cannot produce a false positive. When exact runtime type matters, JUnit also provides `assertThrowsExactly`.

sections.title: Deep Exception Assertions
sections.content:
emerald|Type|~Most specific|assertThrows(T.class, ...)|subtype also passes|avoid superclass
blue|Message|~Inspect text|ex.getMessage()|contains/equals|why it failed
amber|Cause|~Wrapped errors|ex.getCause()|root cause type|service wraps SQL
violet|Custom fields|~Downcast|((AppException) ex).code()|domain-specific|rich assertions

sections.title: Type, Message, Cause, and Custom Fields
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Broad superclass.** `assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, ...)` may accept unrelated failures; use the contract type.
- **Unstable detail checks.** Assert a code, message, field, or cause only when it is part of the behavior being promised.
- **Exact versus subtype.** `assertThrows` accepts subtypes; use `assertThrowsExactly` when exact runtime class is required.
- **Volatile text.** Prefer a stable code or meaningful fragment when full message wording can change.

questions.question: What is the difference between assertEquals and assertSame in JUnit 5?
questions.title: assertEquals vs assertSame JUnit 5 | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: **`assertEquals`** checks **value equality** — it calls the objects' `equals()` method — while **`assertSame`** checks **reference identity** — whether both references point to the **exact same object** (`==`). Two distinct objects with equal fields pass `assertEquals` but fail `assertSame`. You rarely need `assertSame` except for caches, singletons, or interned values.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`assertEquals`** — value equality via `equals()`.
- **`assertSame`** — reference identity via `==`.
- **No `equals()`** → `assertEquals` falls back to identity.
- **Records** auto-implement `equals()` for value comparison.
- **`assertSame`** only for caches/singletons/interning.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The difference is value equality versus reference identity. assertEquals checks that two things are equal by value, and under the hood it calls the equals method. assertSame checks that two references point to the exact same object in memory, which is the double-equals comparison.

So if I create two separate Point objects with the same coordinates, assertEquals will say they're equal — assuming Point overrides equals — but assertSame will fail, because they're two distinct objects even though their fields match. In practice, assertEquals is what I want almost all the time, because I usually care that the values match, not that it's literally the same instance.

There's a subtle trap worth calling out. If a class doesn't override equals, then assertEquals falls back to the default Object equals, which is just identity. So assertEquals on two value-equal objects of a class without an equals override will fail, behaving like assertSame. The fix is to make the class a record, which auto-generates equals, or to override equals manually.

assertSame does have legitimate uses, but they're rare — they're about identity mattering. For example, testing that a cache returns the same cached instance on repeated calls, or that a singleton always hands back the same object, or interned values like enums. In those cases I genuinely want to assert it's the same reference.

sections.title: Value equality and object identity answer different questions
sections.content:
**`assertEquals`** asks whether two values are equal according to `equals`; **`assertSame`** asks whether two references point to one object. That makes `assertEquals` the normal choice for strings, records, value objects, and collections.

For example, two `Point(2, 3)` records are separate instances, so `assertSame` fails, but their generated value equality makes `assertEquals` pass. A class that does not override `equals` inherits identity-based equality from `Object`, so even `assertEquals` then fails for two different instances with identical fields. `assertSame` is useful only when identity is itself the promise, such as a cache returning the previously stored instance or a singleton returning one shared object.

sections.title: assertEquals vs assertSame
sections.content:
emerald|assertEquals|~Value equality|calls equals()|two equal objects pass|the default choice
blue|assertSame|~Reference identity|uses == |must be SAME object|rarely needed
amber|The trap|~No equals() override|assertEquals falls back|to identity|fails value-equal objects
violet|assertSame uses|~Identity matters|caches return same|singletons|interned strings/enums

sections.title: Misusing assertSame for value comparison
Use assertEquals for value; assertSame only for identity
Quick Comparison
sections.content:
| | `assertEquals` | `assertSame` |
|---|---|---|
| Compares | Value (`equals()`) | Reference (`==`) |
| Two equal-but-distinct objects | Pass | Fail |
| Needs `equals()` override | Yes (else identity) | No |
| Typical use | Almost always | Caches, singletons, interning |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`assertSame` for values.** It fails for distinct objects with equal fields; use `assertEquals`.
- **No `equals()` override.** `assertEquals` then compares identity and fails unexpectedly — use a record or override `equals`.
- **Relying on `==` for strings.** String identity depends on interning; compare values with `assertEquals`.
- **Overusing `assertSame`.** Real identity needs are rare (caches, singletons).

questions.question: How do you write a good assertion failure message so the test output is informative?
questions.title: Assertion Failure Messages JUnit 5 | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: JUnit already reports expected and actual values, so add a custom message when it supplies missing context such as the scenario or business rule: `assertEquals(expected, actual, "premium discount")`. In Jupiter assertion overloads the message or `Supplier<String>` comes last; a supplier is evaluated only on failure. AssertJ uses `as(...)` or `describedAs(...)` before the assertion.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Message is LAST** in JUnit 5 (first in JUnit 4).
- **`Supplier<String>`** builds the message lazily, only on failure.
- **Be specific** — scenario plus the relevant values.
- **AssertJ `as("...")`** describes the assertion.
- **Self-explaining failures** save CI debugging time.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: JUnit already shows expected and actual values, so I add a custom message only when it contributes missing context—for example, `assertEquals(90, total, "premium order should receive 10% discount")`. In Jupiter assertion overloads, the optional message comes last. When building it is expensive, I pass a `Supplier<String>` so JUnit evaluates it only if the assertion fails. A clear test name and a precise assertion may already make a custom message unnecessary. With AssertJ, `as(...)` or `describedAs(...)` adds the same kind of context before the final assertion.

sections.title: A failure message should explain the broken rule
sections.content:
JUnit already prints expected and actual values, so a custom message should add the missing context: the scenario or business rule that failed. In JUnit 5 the message is the final argument of an assertion.

For example, `assertEquals(90, total, "premium order should receive 10% discount")` is more useful in CI than `assertEquals(90, total)`, because it identifies the rule without opening the test. Avoid messages that merely repeat “values differ.” When building the message is expensive, pass a `Supplier<String>` such as `() -> render(order)`; JUnit evaluates it only after a failure. AssertJ provides the same descriptive idea through `as(...)` or `describedAs(...)` before the final assertion.

sections.title: Good Failure Messages at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Where|~Last argument (JUnit 5)|assertEquals(exp, act, msg)|JUnit 4 was first|easy to flip
blue|Lazy|~Supplier<String>|() -> expensive()|only built on failure|free when passing
amber|Content|~Be specific|name the scenario|include the values|actionable
violet|AssertJ|~as("...")|describes the check|same intent|fluent style

sections.title: Unhelpful: no message, or message in JUnit 4 position
Helpful: descriptive, lazily-built messages
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **JUnit 4 parameter order.** In Jupiter assertion overloads, the message follows the values or executable.
- **Forcing a message onto every assertion.** A descriptive test name and JUnit's expected/actual output may already be enough.
- **Eager expensive messages.** Use a Supplier when constructing the message has meaningful cost.
- **Restating the assertion.** Add the scenario or rule rather than saying only "values should be equal".

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: A custom message improves a failure only when it adds information that the test name and assertion output do not already provide. Prefer a short business rule or scenario. Use a lazy Supplier for genuinely expensive rendering, but keep the assertion itself readable rather than moving important logic into the message.
